# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.103/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

# bincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bincode/^1.2.1/

## Expand description

Bincode is a crate for encoding and decoding using a tiny binary serialization strategy. Using it, you can easily go from having an object in memory, quickly serialize it to bytes, and then deserialize it back just as fast!

[§](https://docs.rs#using-basic-functions)Using Basic Functions

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    // The object that we will serialize.
    let target: Option<String>  = Some("hello world".to_string());
    let encoded: Vec<u8> = bincode::serialize(&target).unwrap();
    let decoded: Option<String> = bincode::deserialize(&encoded[..]).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(target, decoded);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#128bit-numbers)128bit numbers

Support for `i128` and `u128` is automatically enabled on Rust toolchains
greater than or equal to `1.26.0` and disabled for targets which do not support it

# rand_pcg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_pcg/^0.3.0/

## Expand description

The PCG random number generators.

This is a native Rust implementation of a small selection of PCG generators. The primary goal of this crate is simple, minimal, well-tested code; in other words it is explicitly not a goal to re-implement all of PCG.

This crate provides:

- `Pcg32`aka- `Lcg64Xsh32`, officially known as- `pcg32`, a general purpose RNG. This is a good choice on both 32-bit and 64-bit CPUs (for 32-bit output).
- `Pcg64`aka- `Lcg128Xsl64`, officially known as- `pcg64`, a general purpose RNG. This is a good choice on 64-bit CPUs.
- `Pcg64Mcg`aka- `Mcg128Xsl64`, officially known as- `pcg64_fast`, a general purpose RNG using 128-bit multiplications. This has poor performance on 32-bit CPUs but is a good choice on 64-bit CPUs for both 32-bit and 64-bit output.

Both of these use 16 bytes of state and 128-bit seeds, and are considered value-stable (i.e. any change affecting the output given a fixed seed would be considered a breaking change to the crate).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- A PCG random number generator (XSH RR 64/32 (LCG) variant).
- A PCG random number generator (XSL RR 128/64 (LCG) variant).
- A PCG random number generator (XSL 128/64 (MCG) variant).

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand/latest/target-redirect/rand/

## Expand description

Random-number generators and samplers

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
// rand::random() supports many common types:
println!("Uniform i8 sample: {}", match rand::random() {
    0i8 => "zero",
    i if i > 0 => "positive",
    _ => "negative",
});
// Ranged sampling:
use std::f32::consts::PI;
println!("Angle: {} degrees", rand::random_range(-PI..PI));
```
See also [The Book: Quick Start](https://rust-random.github.io/book/quick-start.html).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [rand_core](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/index.html);

- Return an iterator over `random()`
- [random_](https://docs.rs/fn.random_range.html)- range - `thread_rng`
- Generate a random value in the given range using the thread-local random number generator.
- [random_](https://docs.rs/fn.random_ratio.html)- ratio - `thread_rng`
- Return a bool with a probability of `numerator/denominator`of being true.
- [rng](https://docs.rs/fn.rng.html)- `thread_rng`
- Access a fast, pre-initialized generator

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand/0.8.6/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/rand/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

To get you started quickly, the easiest and highest-level way to get
a random value is to use [ random()](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html); alternatively you can use

[. The](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)

`thread_rng()`[trait provides a useful API on all RNGs, while the](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[and](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)

`distributions`[modules provide further functionality on top of RNGs.](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)

`seq````
use rand::prelude::*;
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    // Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
    println!("char: {}", rand::random::<char>());
}
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let y: f64 = rng.gen(); // generates a float between 0 and 1
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [distributions](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)
- Generating random samples from probability distributions
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Convenience re-export of common members
- [rngs](https://docs.rs/rngs/index.html)
- Random number generators and adapters
- [seq](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)
- Sequence-related functionality

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error type of random number generators

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Crypto](https://docs.rs/trait.CryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait used to indicate that an `RngCore``BlockRngCore`
- [Fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Fill.html)
- Types which may be filled with random data
- [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)
- An automatically-implemented extension trait on `RngCore`
- [RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html)
- The core of a random number generator.
- [Seedable](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html)- Rng
- A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [random](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html)- `std`and- `std_rng`
- Generates a random value using the thread-local random number generator.
- [thread_](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)- rng - `std`and- `std_rng`
- Retrieve the lazily-initialized thread-local random number generator,
seeded by the system. Intended to be used in method chaining style,
e.g. `thread_rng().gen::<i32>()`, or cached locally, e.g.`let mut rng = thread_rng();`. Invoked by the`Default`trait, making`ThreadRng::default()`equivalent.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand/0.8.6/target-redirect/rand/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

To get you started quickly, the easiest and highest-level way to get
a random value is to use [ random()](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html); alternatively you can use

[. The](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)

`thread_rng()`[trait provides a useful API on all RNGs, while the](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[and](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)

`distributions`[modules provide further functionality on top of RNGs.](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)

`seq````
use rand::prelude::*;
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    // Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
    println!("char: {}", rand::random::<char>());
}
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let y: f64 = rng.gen(); // generates a float between 0 and 1
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

# random in rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8.4/fn.random.html

`pub fn random<T>() -> T`**crate features**only.

`std` and `std_rng`## Expand description

Generates a random value using the thread-local random number generator.

This is simply a shortcut for `thread_rng().gen()`. See [ thread_rng](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html) for
documentation of the entropy source and

[for documentation of distributions and type-specific generation.](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.Standard.html)

`Standard`[§](https://docs.rs#provided-implementations)Provided implementations

The following types have provided implementations that generate values with the following ranges and distributions:

- Integers (`i32`,`u32`,`isize`,`usize`, etc.): Uniformly distributed over all values of the type.
- `char`: Uniformly distributed over all Unicode scalar values, i.e. all code points in the range- `0...0x10_FFFF`, except for the range- `0xD800...0xDFFF`(the surrogate code points). This includes unassigned/reserved code points.
- `bool`: Generates- `false`or- `true`, each with probability 0.5.
- Floating point types (`f32`and`f64`): Uniformly distributed in the half-open range`[0, 1)`. See notes below.
- Wrapping integers (`Wrapping<T>`), besides the type identical to their normal integer variants.

Also supported is the generation of the following compound types where all component types are supported:

- Tuples (up to 12 elements): each element is generated sequentially.
- Arrays (up to 32 elements): each element is generated sequentially;
see also `Rng::fill``u32`and smaller types.
- `Option<T>`first generates a- `bool`, and if true generates and returns- `Some(value)`where- `value: T`, otherwise returning- `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let x = rand::random::<u8>();
println!("{}", x);
let y = rand::random::<f64>();
println!("{}", y);
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    println!("Better lucky than good!");
}
```
If you’re calling `random()` in a loop, caching the generator as in the
following example can increase performance.

```
use rand::Rng;
let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];
for x in v.iter_mut() {
    *x = rand::random()
}
// can be made faster by caching thread_rng
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
for x in v.iter_mut() {
    *x = rng.gen();
}
```

}## Expand description

An automatically-implemented extension trait on [ RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html) providing high-level
generic methods for sampling values and other convenience methods.

This is the primary trait to use when generating random values.

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-usage)Generic usage

The basic pattern is `fn foo<R: Rng + ?Sized>(rng: &mut R)`. Some
things are worth noting here:

- Since `Rng: RngCore`and every`RngCore`implements`Rng`, it makes no difference whether we use`R: Rng`or`R: RngCore`.
- The `+ ?Sized`un-bounding allows functions to be called directly on type-erased references; i.e.`foo(r)`where`r: &mut dyn RngCore`. Without this it would be necessary to write`foo(&mut r)`.

An alternative pattern is possible: `fn foo<R: Rng>(rng: R)`. This has some
trade-offs. It allows the argument to be consumed directly without a `&mut`
(which is how `from_rng(thread_rng())` works); also it still works directly
on references (including type-erased references). Unfortunately within the
function `foo` it is not known whether `rng` is a reference type or not,
hence many uses of `rng` require an extra reference, either explicitly
(`distr.sample(&mut rng)`) or implicitly (`rng.gen()`); one may hope the
optimiser can remove redundant references later.

Example:

```
use rand::Rng;
fn foo<R: Rng + ?Sized>(rng: &mut R) -> f32 {
    rng.gen()
}
```
## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Return a random value supporting the [ Standard](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.Standard.html) distribution.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::{thread_rng, Rng};
let mut rng = thread_rng();
let x: u32 = rng.gen();
println!("{}", x);
println!("{:?}", rng.gen::<(f64, bool)>());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#arrays-and-tuples)Arrays and tuples

The `rng.gen()` method is able to generate arrays (up to 32 elements)
and tuples (up to 12 elements), so long as all element types can be
generated.
When using `rustc` ≥ 1.51, enable the `min_const_gen` feature to support
arrays larger than 32 elements.

For arrays of integers, especially for those with small element types
(< 64 bit), it will likely be faster to instead use [ Rng::fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html#method.fill).

```
use rand::{thread_rng, Rng};
let mut rng = thread_rng();
let tuple: (u8, i32, char) = rng.gen(); // arbitrary tuple support
let arr1: [f32; 32] = rng.gen();        // array construction
let mut arr2 = [0u8; 128];
rng.fill(&mut arr2);                    // array fill
```
Generate a random value in the given range.

This function is optimised for the case that only a single sample is
made from the given range. See also the [ Uniform](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.Uniform.html) distribution
type which may be faster if sampling from the same range repeatedly.

Only `gen_range(low..high)` and `gen_range(low..=high)` are supported.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the range is empty.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use rand::{thread_rng, Rng};
let mut rng = thread_rng();
// Exclusive range
let n: u32 = rng.gen_range(0..10);
println!("{}", n);
let m: f64 = rng.gen_range(-40.0..1.3e5);
println!("{}", m);
// Inclusive range
let n: u32 = rng.gen_range(0..=10);
println!("{}", n);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand/rng.rs.html#192-198)#### fn [sample_iter](https://docs.rs#method.sample_iter)<T, D>(self, distr: D) -> [DistIter](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.DistIter.html)<D, Self, T> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand/rng.rs.html#192-198)

#### fn [sample_iter](https://docs.rs#method.sample_iter)<T, D>(self, distr: D) -> [DistIter](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.DistIter.html)<D, Self, T> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

Create an iterator that generates values using the given distribution.

Note that this function takes its arguments by value. This works since
`(&mut R): Rng where R: Rng` and
`(&D): Distribution where D: Distribution`,
however borrowing is not automatic hence `rng.sample_iter(...)` may
need to be replaced with `(&mut rng).sample_iter(...)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
use rand::{thread_rng, Rng};
use rand::distributions::{Alphanumeric, Uniform, Standard};
let mut rng = thread_rng();
// Vec of 16 x f32:
let v: Vec<f32> = (&mut rng).sample_iter(Standard).take(16).collect();
// String:
let s: String = (&mut rng).sample_iter(Alphanumeric)
    .take(7)
    .map(char::from)
    .collect();
// Combined values
println!("{:?}", (&mut rng).sample_iter(Standard).take(5)
                             .collect::<Vec<(f64, bool)>>());
// Dice-rolling:
let die_range = Uniform::new_inclusive(1, 6);
let mut roll_die = (&mut rng).sample_iter(die_range);
while roll_die.next().unwrap() != 6 {
    println!("Not a 6; rolling again!");
}
```
Fill any type implementing [ Fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Fill.html) with random data

The distribution is expected to be uniform with portable results, but this cannot be guaranteed for third-party implementations.

This is identical to [ try_fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html#method.try_fill) except that it panics on error.

```

Return a bool with a probability of `numerator/denominator` of being
true. I.e. `gen_ratio(2, 3)` has chance of 2 in 3, or about 67%, of
returning true. If `numerator == denominator`, then the returned value
is guaranteed to be `true`. If `numerator == 0`, then the returned
value is guaranteed to be `false`.

See also the [ Bernoulli](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.Bernoulli.html) distribution, which may be faster if
sampling from the same

`numerator` and `denominator` repeatedly.[§](https://docs.rs#panics-2)Panics

If `denominator == 0` or `numerator > denominator`.

# CryptoRng in rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8.4/trait.CryptoRng.html

`pub trait CryptoRng { }`## Expand description

A marker trait used to indicate that an [ RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html) or

[implementation is supposed to be cryptographically secure.](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.6.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/block/trait.BlockRngCore.html)

`BlockRngCore`*Cryptographically secure generators*, also known as *CSPRNGs*, should
satisfy an additional properties over other generators: given the first
*k* bits of an algorithm’s output
sequence, it should not be possible using polynomial-time algorithms to
predict the next bit with probability significantly greater than 50%.

Some generators may satisfy an additional property, however this is not
required by this trait: if the CSPRNG’s state is revealed, it should not be
computationally-feasible to reconstruct output prior to this. Some other
generators allow backwards-computation and are considered *reversible*.

Note that this trait is provided for guidance only and cannot guarantee suitability for cryptographic applications. In general it should only be implemented for well-reviewed code implementing well-regarded algorithms.

Note also that use of a `CryptoRng` does not protect against other
weaknesses such as seeding from a weak entropy source or leaking state.

## Implementations on Foreign Types[§](https://docs.rs#foreign-impls)

[Source](https://docs.rs/rand_chacha/0.3.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/rand_chacha/chacha.rs.html#345)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-CryptoRng-for-ChaCha8Core)

# RngCore in rand - Rust

pub trait RngCore {
    // Required methods
    fn
```
[next_u32](https://docs.rs#tymethod.next_u32)(&mut self) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html);
[next_u64](https://docs.rs#tymethod.next_u64)(&mut self) -> [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html);
[fill_bytes](https://docs.rs#tymethod.fill_bytes)(&mut self, dest: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]);

}## Expand description

The core of a random number generator.

This trait encapsulates the low-level functionality common to all
generators, and is the “back end”, to be implemented by generators.
End users should normally use the `Rng` trait from the [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand) crate,
which is automatically implemented for every type implementing

`RngCore`.Three different methods for generating random data are provided since the
optimal implementation of each is dependent on the type of generator. There
is no required relationship between the output of each; e.g. many
implementations of [ fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.fill_bytes) consume a whole number of

`u32` or `u64`
values and drop any remaining unused bytes. The same can happen with the
[and](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.next_u32)

`next_u32`[methods, implementations may discard some random bits for efficiency.](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.next_u64)

`next_u64`The [ try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.try_fill_bytes) method is a variant of

[allowing error handling; it is not deemed sufficiently useful to add equivalents for](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.fill_bytes)

`fill_bytes`[or](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.next_u32)

`next_u32`[since the latter methods are almost always used with algorithmic generators (PRNGs), which are normally infallible.](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.next_u64)

`next_u64`Implementers should produce bits uniformly. Pathological RNGs (e.g. always
returning the same value, or never setting certain bits) can break rejection
sampling used by random distributions, and also break other RNGs when
seeding them via [ SeedableRng::from_rng](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html#method.from_rng).

Algorithmic generators implementing [ SeedableRng](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html) should normally have

*portable, reproducible*output, i.e. fix Endianness when converting values to avoid platform differences, and avoid making any changes which affect output (except by communicating that the release has breaking changes).

Typically an RNG will implement only one of the methods available
in this trait directly, then use the helper functions from the
[ impls](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.6.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/impls/index.html) module to implement the other methods.

It is recommended that implementations also implement:

- `Debug`with a custom implementation which- *does not*print any internal state (at least,- `CryptoRng`- `Debug`).
- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`(from Serde), preferably making Serde support optional at the crate level in PRNG libs.
- `Clone`, if possible.
- *never*implement- `Copy`(accidental copies may cause repeated values).
- *do not*implement- `Default`for pseudorandom generators, but instead implement- `SeedableRng`- `Default`.
- `Eq`and- `PartialEq`could be implemented, but are probably not useful.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

A simple example, obviously not generating very *random* output:

```
#![allow(dead_code)]
use rand_core::{RngCore, Error, impls};
struct CountingRng(u64);
impl RngCore for CountingRng {
    fn next_u32(&mut self) -> u32 {
        self.next_u64() as u32
    }
    fn next_u64(&mut self) -> u64 {
        self.0 += 1;
        self.0
    }
    fn fill_bytes(&mut self, dest: &mut [u8]) {
        impls::fill_bytes_via_next(self, dest)
    }
    fn try_fill_bytes(&mut self, dest: &mut [u8]) -> Result<(), Error> {
        Ok(self.fill_bytes(dest))
    }
}
```

Fill `dest` with random data.

`RngCore::try_fill_bytes`This method should guarantee that `dest` is entirely filled
with new data, and may panic if this is impossible
(e.g. reading past the end of a file that is being used as the
source of randomness).

Fill `dest` entirely with random data.

This is the only method which allows an RNG to report errors while
generating random data thus making this the primary method implemented
by external (true) RNGs (e.g. `OsRng`) which can fail. It may be used
directly to generate keys and to seed (infallible) PRNGs.

Other than error handling, this method is identical to [ RngCore::fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.fill_bytes);
thus this may be implemented using

`Ok(self.fill_bytes(dest))` or
`fill_bytes` may be implemented with

# SeedableRng in rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8.4/trait.SeedableRng.html

[from_entropy](https://docs.rs#method.from_entropy)() -> Self { ... }
}## Expand description

A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.

This trait encapsulates the low-level functionality common to all pseudo-random number generators (PRNGs, or algorithmic generators).

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

Seed type, which is restricted to types mutably-dereferenceable as `u8`
arrays (we recommend `[u8; N]` for some `N`).

It is recommended to seed PRNGs with a seed of at least circa 100 bits,
which means an array of `[u8; 12]` or greater to avoid picking RNGs with
partially overlapping periods.

For cryptographic RNG’s a seed of 256 bits is recommended, `[u8; 32]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-seedablerng-for-rngs-with-large-seeds)Implementing `SeedableRng` for RNGs with large seeds

Note that the required traits `core::default::Default` and
`core::convert::AsMut<u8>` are not implemented for large arrays
`[u8; N]` with `N` > 32. To be able to implement the traits required by
`SeedableRng` for RNGs with such large seeds, the newtype pattern can be
used:

```
use rand_core::SeedableRng;
const N: usize = 64;
pub struct MyRngSeed(pub [u8; N]);
pub struct MyRng(MyRngSeed);
impl Default for MyRngSeed {
    fn default() -> MyRngSeed {
        MyRngSeed([0; N])
    }
}
impl AsMut<[u8]> for MyRngSeed {
    fn as_mut(&mut self) -> &mut [u8] {
        &mut self.0
    }
}
impl SeedableRng for MyRng {
    type Seed = MyRngSeed;
    fn from_seed(seed: MyRngSeed) -> MyRng {
        MyRng(seed)
    }
}
```
## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Create a new PRNG using the given seed.

PRNG implementations are allowed to assume that bits in the seed are
well distributed. That means usually that the number of one and zero
bits are roughly equal, and values like 0, 1 and (size - 1) are unlikely.
Note that many non-cryptographic PRNGs will show poor quality output
if this is not adhered to. If you wish to seed from simple numbers, use
`seed_from_u64` instead.

All PRNG implementations should be reproducible unless otherwise noted:
given a fixed `seed`, the same sequence of output should be produced
on all runs, library versions and architectures (e.g. check endianness).
Any “value-breaking” changes to the generator should require bumping at
least the minor version and documentation of the change.

It is not required that this function yield the same state as a reference implementation of the PRNG given equivalent seed; if necessary another constructor replicating behaviour from a reference implementation can be added.

PRNG implementations should make sure `from_seed` never panics. In the
case that some special values (like an all zero seed) are not viable
seeds it is preferable to map these to alternative constant value(s),
for example `0xBAD5EEDu32` or `0x0DDB1A5E5BAD5EEDu64` (“odd biases? bad
seed”). This is assuming only a small number of values must be rejected.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.6.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/rand_core/lib.rs.html#335)#### fn [seed_from_u64](https://docs.rs#method.seed_from_u64)(state: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.6.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/rand_core/lib.rs.html#335)

#### fn [seed_from_u64](https://docs.rs#method.seed_from_u64)(state: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)) -> Self

Create a new PRNG using a `u64` seed.

This is a convenience-wrapper around `from_seed` to allow construction
of any `SeedableRng` from a simple `u64` value. It is designed such that
low Hamming Weight numbers like 0 and 1 can be used and should still
result in good, independent seeds to the PRNG which is returned.

This **is not suitable for cryptography**, as should be clear given that
the input size is only 64 bits.

Implementations for PRNGs *may* provide their own implementations of
this function, but the default implementation should be good enough for
all purposes. *Changing* the implementation of this function should be
considered a value-breaking change.

Create a new PRNG seeded from another `Rng`.

This may be useful when needing to rapidly seed many PRNGs from a master PRNG, and to allow forking of PRNGs. It may be considered deterministic.

The master PRNG should be at least as high quality as the child PRNGs.
When seeding non-cryptographic child PRNGs, we recommend using a
different algorithm for the master PRNG (ideally a CSPRNG) to avoid
correlations between the child PRNGs. If this is not possible (e.g.
forking using small non-crypto PRNGs) ensure that your PRNG has a good
mixing function on the output or consider use of a hash function with
`from_seed`.

Note that seeding `XorShiftRng` from another `XorShiftRng` provides an
extreme example of what can go wrong: the new PRNG will be a clone
of the parent.

PRNG implementations are allowed to assume that a good RNG is provided
for seeding, and that it is cryptographically secure when appropriate.
As of `rand` 0.7 / `rand_core` 0.5, implementations overriding this
method should ensure the implementation satisfies reproducibility
(in prior versions this was not required).

[Source](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.6.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/rand_core/lib.rs.html#412)

#### fn [from_entropy](https://docs.rs#method.from_entropy)() -> Self

**crate feature**only.

`getrandom`Creates a new instance of the RNG seeded via [ getrandom](https://docs.rs/getrandom).

This method is the recommended way to construct non-deterministic PRNGs since it is convenient and secure.

In case the overhead of using [ getrandom](https://docs.rs/getrandom) to seed

*many*PRNGs is an issue, one may prefer to seed from a local PRNG, e.g.

`from_rng(thread_rng()).unwrap()`.[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

If [ getrandom](https://docs.rs/getrandom) is unable to provide secure entropy this method will panic.

# rand_xorshift 0.3.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_xorshift/0.3.0

# rand_xorshift

Implements the Xorshift random number generator.

The Xorshift[^1] algorithm is not suitable for cryptographic purposes
but is very fast. If you do not know for sure that it fits your
requirements, use a more secure one such as `StdRng` or `OsRng`.

[^1]: Marsaglia, George (July 2003).
["Xorshift RNGs"](https://www.jstatsoft.org/v08/i14/paper).
*Journal of Statistical Software*. Vol. 8 (Issue 14).

## Crate Features

`rand_xorshift` is `no_std` compatible. It does not require any functionality
outside of the `core` lib, thus there are no features to configure.

The `serde1` feature includes implementations of `Serialize` and `Deserialize`
for the included RNGs.

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.118/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

# bincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bincode/^1/

## Expand description

Bincode is a crate for encoding and decoding using a tiny binary serialization strategy. Using it, you can easily go from having an object in memory, quickly serialize it to bytes, and then deserialize it back just as fast!

[§](https://docs.rs#using-basic-functions)Using Basic Functions

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    // The object that we will serialize.
    let target: Option<String>  = Some("hello world".to_string());
    let encoded: Vec<u8> = bincode::serialize(&target).unwrap();
    let decoded: Option<String> = bincode::deserialize(&encoded[..]).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(target, decoded);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#128bit-numbers)128bit numbers

Support for `i128` and `u128` is automatically enabled on Rust toolchains
greater than or equal to `1.26.0` and disabled for targets which do not support it

# typed-arena 2.0.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/typed-arena/2.0.2

`typed-arena`

**A fast (but limited) allocation arena for values of a single type.**

Allocated objects are destroyed all at once, when the arena itself is destroyed. There is no deallocation of individual objects while the arena itself is still alive. The flipside is that allocation is fast: typically just a vector push.

There is also a method `into_vec()` to recover ownership of allocated objects
when the arena is no longer required, instead of destroying everything.

## Example

```
use Arena;
let monsters = new;
let goku = monsters.alloc;
assert!;
```
## Safe Cycles

All allocated objects get the same lifetime, so you can safely create cycles between them. This can be useful for certain data structures, such as graphs and trees with parent pointers.

```
use Cell;
use Arena;
let arena = new;
let a = arena.alloc;
let b = arena.alloc;
a.other.set;
b.other.set;
```
## Alternatives

### Need to allocate many different types of values?

Use multiple arenas if you have only a couple different types or try
[ bumpalo](https://crates.io/crates/bumpalo), which is a bump-allocation arena
can allocate heterogenous types of values.

### Want allocation to return identifiers instead of references and dealing with references and lifetimes everywhere?

Check out [ id-arena](https://crates.io/crates/id-arena) or

[.](https://crates.io/crates/generational-arena)

`generational-arena`### Need to deallocate individual objects at a time?

Check out [ generational-arena](https://crates.io/crates/generational-arena)
for an arena-style crate or look for a more traditional allocator.

# typed_arena - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/typed-arena/2.0.2/target-redirect/typed_arena/

## Expand description

The arena, a fast but limited type of allocator.

**A fast (but limited) allocation arena for values of a single type.**

Allocated objects are destroyed all at once, when the arena itself is destroyed. There is no deallocation of individual objects while the arena itself is still alive. The flipside is that allocation is fast: typically just a vector push.

There is also a method `into_vec()` to recover ownership of allocated
objects when the arena is no longer required, instead of destroying
everything.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use typed_arena::Arena;
struct Monster {
    level: u32,
}
let monsters = Arena::new();
let goku = monsters.alloc(Monster { level: 9001 });
assert!(goku.level > 9000);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#safe-cycles)Safe Cycles

All allocated objects get the same lifetime, so you can safely create cycles between them. This can be useful for certain data structures, such as graphs and trees with parent pointers.

```
use std::cell::Cell;
use typed_arena::Arena;
struct CycleParticipant<'a> {
    other: Cell<Option<&'a CycleParticipant<'a>>>,
}
let arena = Arena::new();
let a = arena.alloc(CycleParticipant { other: Cell::new(None) });
let b = arena.alloc(CycleParticipant { other: Cell::new(None) });
a.other.set(Some(b));
b.other.set(Some(a));
```

Allocates space for a given number of values, but doesn’t initialize it.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

After calling this method, the arena considers the elements initialized. If you fail to initialize them (which includes because of panicking during the initialization), the arena will run destructors on the uninitialized memory. Therefore, you must initialize them.

Considering how easy it is to cause undefined behaviour using this, you’re advised to
prefer the other (safe) methods, like [ alloc_extend](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.alloc_extend).

[§](https://docs.rs#example-6)Example

```
use std::mem::{self, MaybeUninit};
use std::ptr;
use typed_arena::Arena;
// Transmute from MaybeUninit slice to slice of initialized T.
// It is a separate function to preserve the lifetime of the reference.
unsafe fn transmute_uninit<A>(r: &mut [MaybeUninit<A>]) -> &mut [A] {
    mem::transmute(r)
}
let arena: Arena<bool> = Arena::new();
let slice: &mut [bool];
unsafe {
    let uninitialized = arena.alloc_uninitialized(10);
    for elem in uninitialized.iter_mut() {
        ptr::write(elem.as_mut_ptr(), true);
    }
    slice = transmute_uninit(uninitialized);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#alternative-allocation-pattern)Alternative allocation pattern

To avoid the problem of dropping assumed to be initialized elements on panic, it is also
possible to combine the [ reserve_extend](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.reserve_extend) with

[, initialize the elements and confirm them by this method. In such case, when there’s a panic during initialization, the already initialized elements would leak but it wouldn’t cause UB.](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.uninitialized_array)

`uninitialized_array````
use std::mem::{self, MaybeUninit};
use std::ptr;
use typed_arena::Arena;
unsafe fn transmute_uninit<A>(r: &mut [MaybeUninit<A>]) -> &mut [A] {
    mem::transmute(r)
}
const COUNT: usize = 2;
let arena: Arena<String> = Arena::new();
arena.reserve_extend(COUNT);
let slice: &mut [String];
unsafe {
    // Perform initialization before we claim the memory.
    let uninitialized = arena.uninitialized_array();
    assert!((*uninitialized).len() >= COUNT); // Ensured by the reserve_extend
    for elem in &mut (*uninitialized)[..COUNT] {
        ptr::write(elem.as_mut_ptr(), "Hello".to_owned());
    }
    let addr = (*uninitialized).as_ptr() as usize;
    // The alloc_uninitialized returns the same memory, but "confirms" its allocation.
    slice = transmute_uninit(arena.alloc_uninitialized(COUNT));
    assert_eq!(addr, slice.as_ptr() as usize);
    assert_eq!(slice, &["Hello".to_owned(), "Hello".to_owned()]);
}
```

Convert this `Arena` into a `Vec<T>`.

Items in the resulting `Vec<T>` appear in the order that they were
allocated in.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-7)Example

```
use typed_arena::Arena;
let arena = Arena::new();

arena.alloc("c");

```
Returns an iterator that allows modifying each value.

Items are yielded in the order that they were allocated.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-8)Example

```
use typed_arena::Arena;
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 };
let mut arena = Arena::new();
arena.alloc(Point { x: 0, y: 0 });
arena.alloc(Point { x: 1, y: 1 });
for point in arena.iter_mut() {
    point.x += 10;
}
let points = arena.into_vec();

```

# intrusive_collections - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/intrusive-collections/latest/target-redirect/intrusive_collections/index.html

## Expand description

Intrusive collections for Rust.

This library provides a set of high-performance intrusive collections which can offer better performance and more flexibility than standard collections.

The main difference between an intrusive collection and a normal one is that
while normal collections allocate memory behind your back to keep track of a
set of *values*, intrusive collections never allocate memory themselves and
instead keep track of a set of *objects*. Such collections are called
intrusive because they requires explicit support in objects to allow them to
be inserted into a collection.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use intrusive_collections::intrusive_adapter;
use intrusive_collections::{LinkedList, LinkedListLink};
use std::cell::Cell;
// A simple struct containing an instrusive link and a value
struct Test {
    link: LinkedListLink,
    value: Cell<i32>,
}
// The adapter describes how an object can be inserted into an intrusive
// collection. This is automatically generated using a macro.
intrusive_adapter!(TestAdapter = Box<Test>: Test { link => LinkedListLink });
// Create a list and some objects
let mut list = LinkedList::new(TestAdapter::new());
let a = Box::new(Test {
    link: LinkedListLink::new(),
    value: Cell::new(1),
});
let b = Box::new(Test {
    link: LinkedListLink::new(),
    value: Cell::new(2),
});
let c = Box::new(Test {
    link: LinkedListLink::new(),
    value: Cell::new(3),
});
// Insert the objects at the front of the list
list.push_front(a);
list.push_front(b);
list.push_front(c);
assert_eq!(list.iter().map(|x| x.value.get()).collect::<Vec<_>>(), [3, 2, 1]);
// At this point, the objects are owned by the list, and we can modify
// them through the list.
list.front().get().unwrap().value.set(4);
assert_eq!(list.iter().map(|x| x.value.get()).collect::<Vec<_>>(), [4, 2, 1]);
// Removing an object from an instrusive collection gives us back the
// Box<Test> that we originally inserted into it.
let a = list.pop_front().unwrap();
assert_eq!(a.value.get(), 4);
assert_eq!(list.iter().map(|x| x.value.get()).collect::<Vec<_>>(), [2, 1]);
// Dropping the collection will automatically free b and c by
// transforming them back into Box<Test> and dropping them.
drop(list);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#links-and-adapters)Links and adapters

Intrusive collections track objects through links which are embedded within the objects themselves. It also allows a single object to be part of multiple intrusive collections at once by having multiple links in it.

The relationship between an object and a link inside it is described by the
`Adapter` trait. Intrusive collections use an implementation of this trait
to determine which link in an object should be used by the collection. In
most cases you do not need to write an implementation manually: the
`intrusive_adapter!` macro will automatically generate the necessary code.

For red-black trees, the adapter must also implement the `KeyAdapter` trait
which allows a key to be extracted from an object. This key is then used to
keep all elements in the tree in ascending order.

```
use intrusive_collections::intrusive_adapter;
use intrusive_collections::{SinglyLinkedListLink, SinglyLinkedList};
use intrusive_collections::{LinkedListLink, LinkedList};
use intrusive_collections::{XorLinkedList, XorLinkedListLink};
use intrusive_collections::{RBTreeLink, RBTree, KeyAdapter};
use std::rc::Rc;
// This struct can be inside three lists and one tree simultaneously
#[derive(Default)]
struct Test {
    link: LinkedListLink,
    link2: SinglyLinkedListLink,
    link3: XorLinkedListLink,
    link4: RBTreeLink,
    value: i32,
}
intrusive_adapter!(MyAdapter = Rc<Test>: Test { link => LinkedListLink });
intrusive_adapter!(MyAdapter2 = Rc<Test>: Test { link2 => SinglyLinkedListLink });
intrusive_adapter!(MyAdapter3 = Rc<Test>: Test { link3 => XorLinkedListLink });
intrusive_adapter!(MyAdapter4 = Rc<Test>: Test { link4 => RBTreeLink });
impl<'a> KeyAdapter<'a> for MyAdapter4 {
    type Key = i32;
    fn get_key(&self, x: &'a Test) -> i32 { x.value }
}
let mut a = LinkedList::new(MyAdapter::new());
let mut b = SinglyLinkedList::new(MyAdapter2::new());
let mut c = XorLinkedList::new(MyAdapter3::new());
let mut d = RBTree::new(MyAdapter4::new());
let test = Rc::new(Test::default());
a.push_front(test.clone());
b.push_front(test.clone());
c.push_front(test.clone());
d.insert(test);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#cursors)Cursors

Intrusive collections are manipulated using cursors. A cursor is similar to an iterator, except that it can freely seek back-and-forth, and can safely mutate the list during iteration. This is similar to how a C++ iterator works.

A cursor views an intrusive collection as a circular list, with a special null object between the last and first elements of the collection. A cursor will either point to a valid object in the collection or to this special null object.

Cursors come in two forms: `Cursor` and `CursorMut`. A `Cursor` gives a
read-only view of a collection, but you are allowed to use multiple `Cursor`
objects simultaneously on the same collection. On the other hand,
`CursorMut` can be used to mutate the collection, but you may only use one
of them at a time.

Use `get` to access the current element by reference, or `get_ptr` to obtain
the raw pointer for pointer identity or FFI interop. Both return `None` when
the cursor is pointing at the null position.

Cursors are a very powerful abstraction since they allow a collection to be
mutated safely while it is being iterated on. For example, here is a
function which removes all values within a given range from a `RBTree`:

```
use intrusive_collections::intrusive_adapter;
use intrusive_collections::{RBTreeLink, RBTree, KeyAdapter, Bound};
struct Element {
    link: RBTreeLink,
    value: i32,
}
intrusive_adapter!(ElementAdapter = Box<Element>: Element { link => RBTreeLink });
impl<'a> KeyAdapter<'a> for ElementAdapter {
    type Key = i32;
    fn get_key(&self, e: &'a Element) -> i32 { e.value }
}
fn remove_range(tree: &mut RBTree<ElementAdapter>, min: i32, max: i32) {
    // Find the first element which is greater than or equal to min
    let mut cursor = tree.lower_bound_mut(Bound::Included(&min));
    // Iterate over all elements in the range [min, max]
    while cursor.get().map_or(false, |e| e.value <= max) {
        // CursorMut::remove will return a Some(<Box<Element>), which we
        // simply drop here. This will also advance the cursor to the next
        // element.
        cursor.remove();
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#scoped-collections)Scoped collections

Instead of taking ownership of objects inserted into them, intrusive collections can also work with borrowed values. This works by using lifetimes and the borrow checker to ensure that any objects inserted into an intrusive collection will outlive the collection itself.

```
use intrusive_collections::intrusive_adapter;
use intrusive_collections::{LinkedListLink, LinkedList};
use typed_arena::Arena;
use std::cell::Cell;
struct Value {
    link: LinkedListLink,
    value: Cell<i32>,
}
// Note that we use a plain reference as the pointer type for the collection.
intrusive_adapter!(ValueAdapter<'a> = &'a Value: Value { link => LinkedListLink });
// Create an arena and a list. Note that since stack objects are dropped in
// reverse order, the Arena must be created before the LinkedList. This
// ensures that the list is dropped before the values are freed by the
// arena. This is enforced by the Rust lifetime system.
let arena = Arena::new();
let mut list = LinkedList::new(ValueAdapter::new());
// We can now insert values allocated from the arena into the linked list
list.push_back(arena.alloc(Value {
    link: LinkedListLink::new(),
    value: Cell::new(1),
}));
list.push_back(arena.alloc(Value {
    link: LinkedListLink::new(),
    value: Cell::new(2),
}));
list.push_back(arena.alloc(Value {
    link: LinkedListLink::new(),
    value: Cell::new(3),
}));
assert_eq!(list.iter().map(|x| x.value.get()).collect::<Vec<_>>(), [1, 2, 3]);
// We can also insert stack allocated values into an intrusive list.
// Again, the values must outlive the LinkedList.
let a = Value {
    link: LinkedListLink::new(),
    value: Cell::new(4),
};
let b = Value {
    link: LinkedListLink::new(),
    value: Cell::new(5),
};
let c = Value {
    link: LinkedListLink::new(),
    value: Cell::new(6),
};
let mut list2 = LinkedList::new(ValueAdapter::new());
list2.push_back(&a);
list2.push_back(&b);
list2.push_back(&c);
assert_eq!(list2.iter().map(|x| x.value.get()).collect::<Vec<_>>(), [4, 5, 6]);
// Since these are shared references, any changes in the values are reflected in
// the list.
a.value.set(7);
assert_eq!(list2.iter().map(|x| x.value.get()).collect::<Vec<_>>(), [7, 5, 6]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

While it is possible to use intrusive collections without any unsafe code, this crate also exposes a few unsafe features.

The `cursor_from_ptr` and `cursor_mut_from_ptr` allow you to create a
cursor pointing to a specific element in the collection from a pointer to
that element. This is unsafe because it assumes that the objected pointed to
is currently inserted in the collection.

The `UnsafeRef` type acts like `Rc`, except without the reference count.
Instead, you are responsible for keeping track of the number of active
references to an object and for freeing it once the last reference is
dropped. The advantage of `UnsafeRef` over `Rc` is that it reduces the size
of the allocation by two `usize` and avoids the overhead of maintaining
reference counts.

- [intrusive_](https://docs.rs/macro.intrusive_adapter.html)- adapter
- Macro to generate an implementation of `Adapter`for a given set of types. In particular this will automatically generate implementations of the`get_value`and`get_link`methods for a given named field in a struct.
- [offset_](https://docs.rs/macro.offset_of.html)- of
- Calculates the offset of the specified field from the start of the named struct.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Default](https://docs.rs/struct.DefaultPointerOps.html)- Pointer - Ops
- The `PointerOps`type used by an`Adapter`generated by`intrusive_adapter!`.
- [Unsafe](https://docs.rs/struct.UnsafeRef.html)- Ref
- Unchecked shared pointer

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Bound](https://docs.rs/enum.Bound.html)
- An endpoint of a range of keys.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Adapter](https://docs.rs/trait.Adapter.html)
- Trait for a adapter which allows a type to be inserted into an intrusive collection.
- [Default](https://docs.rs/trait.DefaultLinkOps.html)- Link - Ops
- The default implementation of `LinkOps`associated with a link type.
- [KeyAdapter](https://docs.rs/trait.KeyAdapter.html)
- Extension of the `Adapter`trait to provide a way of extracting a key from an object. This key can then be used as an index in certain intrusive collections (currently only`RBTree`uses this).
- [LinkOps](https://docs.rs/trait.LinkOps.html)
- Base trait for link operations.
- [Pointer](https://docs.rs/trait.PointerOps.html)- Ops
- Trait for pointer conversion operations.

# intrusive_collections/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)// Copyright 2016 Amanieu d'Antras
[2](https://docs.rs#2)// Copyright 2020 Amari Robinson
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//
[4](https://docs.rs#4)// Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0, <LICENSE-APACHE or
[5](https://docs.rs#5)// http://apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0> or the MIT license <LICENSE-MIT or
[6](https://docs.rs#6)// http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT>, at your option. This file may not be
[7](https://docs.rs#7)// copied, modified, or distributed except according to those terms.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! Intrusive collections for Rust.
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! This library provides a set of high-performance intrusive collections which
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! can offer better performance and more flexibility than standard collections.
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! The main difference between an intrusive collection and a normal one is that
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! while normal collections allocate memory behind your back to keep track of a
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! set of *values*, intrusive collections never allocate memory themselves and
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! instead keep track of a set of *objects*. Such collections are called
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! intrusive because they requires explicit support in objects to allow them to
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! be inserted into a collection.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! # Example
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! ```
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! use intrusive_collections::intrusive_adapter;
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! use intrusive_collections::{LinkedList, LinkedListLink};
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! use std::cell::Cell;
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! // A simple struct containing an instrusive link and a value
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! struct Test {
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!     link: LinkedListLink,
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!     value: Cell<i32>,
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! }
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! // The adapter describes how an object can be inserted into an intrusive
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! // collection. This is automatically generated using a macro.
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! intrusive_adapter!(TestAdapter = Box<Test>: Test { link => LinkedListLink });
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! // Create a list and some objects
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! let mut list = LinkedList::new(TestAdapter::new());
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! let a = Box::new(Test {
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!     link: LinkedListLink::new(),
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!     value: Cell::new(1),
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! });
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! let b = Box::new(Test {
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!     link: LinkedListLink::new(),
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!     value: Cell::new(2),
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! });
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! let c = Box::new(Test {
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!     link: LinkedListLink::new(),
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!     value: Cell::new(3),
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! });
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! // Insert the objects at the front of the list
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! list.push_front(a);
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! list.push_front(b);
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! list.push_front(c);
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! assert_eq!(list.iter().map(|x| x.value.get()).collect::<Vec<_>>(), [3, 2, 1]);
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! // At this point, the objects are owned by the list, and we can modify
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! // them through the list.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! list.front().get().unwrap().value.set(4);
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! assert_eq!(list.iter().map(|x| x.value.get()).collect::<Vec<_>>(), [4, 2, 1]);
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! // Removing an object from an instrusive collection gives us back the
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! // Box<Test> that we originally inserted into it.
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! let a = list.pop_front().unwrap();
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! assert_eq!(a.value.get(), 4);
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! assert_eq!(list.iter().map(|x| x.value.get()).collect::<Vec<_>>(), [2, 1]);
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! // Dropping the collection will automatically free b and c by
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! // transforming them back into Box<Test> and dropping them.
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! drop(list);
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! ```
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! # Links and adapters
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! Intrusive collections track objects through links which are embedded within
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! the objects themselves. It also allows a single object to be part of
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! multiple intrusive collections at once by having multiple links in it.
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! The relationship between an object and a link inside it is described by the
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! `Adapter` trait. Intrusive collections use an implementation of this trait
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! to determine which link in an object should be used by the collection. In
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! most cases you do not need to write an implementation manually: the
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! `intrusive_adapter!` macro will automatically generate the necessary code.
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! For red-black trees, the adapter must also implement the `KeyAdapter` trait
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! which allows a key to be extracted from an object. This key is then used to
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! keep all elements in the tree in ascending order.
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! ```
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! use intrusive_collections::intrusive_adapter;
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! use intrusive_collections::{SinglyLinkedListLink, SinglyLinkedList};
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! use intrusive_collections::{LinkedListLink, LinkedList};
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! use intrusive_collections::{XorLinkedList, XorLinkedListLink};
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! use intrusive_collections::{RBTreeLink, RBTree, KeyAdapter};
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! use std::rc::Rc;
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! // This struct can be inside three lists and one tree simultaneously
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! #[derive(Default)]
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! struct Test {
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//!     link: LinkedListLink,
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!     link2: SinglyLinkedListLink,
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//!     link3: XorLinkedListLink,
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!     link4: RBTreeLink,
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!     value: i32,
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! }
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! intrusive_adapter!(MyAdapter = Rc<Test>: Test { link => LinkedListLink });
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! intrusive_adapter!(MyAdapter2 = Rc<Test>: Test { link2 => SinglyLinkedListLink });
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! intrusive_adapter!(MyAdapter3 = Rc<Test>: Test { link3 => XorLinkedListLink });
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! intrusive_adapter!(MyAdapter4 = Rc<Test>: Test { link4 => RBTreeLink });
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! impl<'a> KeyAdapter<'a> for MyAdapter4 {
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!     type Key = i32;
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!     fn get_key(&self, x: &'a Test) -> i32 { x.value }
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! }
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! let mut a = LinkedList::new(MyAdapter::new());
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! let mut b = SinglyLinkedList::new(MyAdapter2::new());
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! let mut c = XorLinkedList::new(MyAdapter3::new());
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! let mut d = RBTree::new(MyAdapter4::new());
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! let test = Rc::new(Test::default());
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! a.push_front(test.clone());
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! b.push_front(test.clone());
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! c.push_front(test.clone());
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! d.insert(test);
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! ```
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! # Cursors
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! Intrusive collections are manipulated using cursors. A cursor is similar to
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! an iterator, except that it can freely seek back-and-forth, and can safely
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! mutate the list during iteration. This is similar to how a C++ iterator
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! works.
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! A cursor views an intrusive collection as a circular list, with a special
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! null object between the last and first elements of the collection. A cursor
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! will either point to a valid object in the collection or to this special
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! null object.
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! Cursors come in two forms: `Cursor` and `CursorMut`. A `Cursor` gives a
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! read-only view of a collection, but you are allowed to use multiple `Cursor`
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! objects simultaneously on the same collection. On the other hand,
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! `CursorMut` can be used to mutate the collection, but you may only use one
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! of them at a time.
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! Use `get` to access the current element by reference, or `get_ptr` to obtain
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! the raw pointer for pointer identity or FFI interop. Both return `None` when
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! the cursor is pointing at the null position.
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//!
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! Cursors are a very powerful abstraction since they allow a collection to be
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! mutated safely while it is being iterated on. For example, here is a
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! function which removes all values within a given range from a `RBTree`:
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! ```
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! use intrusive_collections::intrusive_adapter;
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! use intrusive_collections::{RBTreeLink, RBTree, KeyAdapter, Bound};
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! struct Element {
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!     link: RBTreeLink,
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!     value: i32,
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! }
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//!
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! intrusive_adapter!(ElementAdapter = Box<Element>: Element { link => RBTreeLink });
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! impl<'a> KeyAdapter<'a> for ElementAdapter {
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//!     type Key = i32;
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!     fn get_key(&self, e: &'a Element) -> i32 { e.value }
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! }
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//!
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! fn remove_range(tree: &mut RBTree<ElementAdapter>, min: i32, max: i32) {
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//!     // Find the first element which is greater than or equal to min
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//!     let mut cursor = tree.lower_bound_mut(Bound::Included(&min));
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//!
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//!     // Iterate over all elements in the range [min, max]
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//!     while cursor.get().map_or(false, |e| e.value <= max) {
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//!         // CursorMut::remove will return a Some(<Box<Element>), which we
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//!         // simply drop here. This will also advance the cursor to the next
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!         // element.
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//!         cursor.remove();
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//!     }
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! }
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! ```
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//!
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! # Scoped collections
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//!
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! Instead of taking ownership of objects inserted into them, intrusive
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! collections can also work with borrowed values. This works by using
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! lifetimes and the borrow checker to ensure that any objects inserted into an
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! intrusive collection will outlive the collection itself.
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! ```
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! use intrusive_collections::intrusive_adapter;
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! use intrusive_collections::{LinkedListLink, LinkedList};
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! use typed_arena::Arena;
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! use std::cell::Cell;
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//!
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! struct Value {
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//!     link: LinkedListLink,
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//!     value: Cell<i32>,
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! }
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! // Note that we use a plain reference as the pointer type for the collection.
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! intrusive_adapter!(ValueAdapter<'a> = &'a Value: Value { link => LinkedListLink });
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//!
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! // Create an arena and a list. Note that since stack objects are dropped in
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! // reverse order, the Arena must be created before the LinkedList. This
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! // ensures that the list is dropped before the values are freed by the
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! // arena. This is enforced by the Rust lifetime system.
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//! let arena = Arena::new();
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! let mut list = LinkedList::new(ValueAdapter::new());
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//!
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! // We can now insert values allocated from the arena into the linked list
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//! list.push_back(arena.alloc(Value {
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//!     link: LinkedListLink::new(),
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//!     value: Cell::new(1),
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! }));
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! list.push_back(arena.alloc(Value {
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//!     link: LinkedListLink::new(),
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//!     value: Cell::new(2),
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! }));
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! list.push_back(arena.alloc(Value {
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//!     link: LinkedListLink::new(),
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//!     value: Cell::new(3),
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! }));
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! assert_eq!(list.iter().map(|x| x.value.get()).collect::<Vec<_>>(), [1, 2, 3]);
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//!
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! // We can also insert stack allocated values into an intrusive list.
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! // Again, the values must outlive the LinkedList.
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! let a = Value {
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//!     link: LinkedListLink::new(),
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//!     value: Cell::new(4),
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//! };
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//! let b = Value {
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//!     link: LinkedListLink::new(),
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//!     value: Cell::new(5),
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! };
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! let c = Value {
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//!     link: LinkedListLink::new(),
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//!     value: Cell::new(6),
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! };
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! let mut list2 = LinkedList::new(ValueAdapter::new());
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//! list2.push_back(&a);
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//! list2.push_back(&b);
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! list2.push_back(&c);
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! assert_eq!(list2.iter().map(|x| x.value.get()).collect::<Vec<_>>(), [4, 5, 6]);
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//!
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! // Since these are shared references, any changes in the values are reflected in
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//! // the list.
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! a.value.set(7);
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! assert_eq!(list2.iter().map(|x| x.value.get()).collect::<Vec<_>>(), [7, 5, 6]);
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//! ```
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//!
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! # Safety
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//!
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//! While it is possible to use intrusive collections without any unsafe code,
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! this crate also exposes a few unsafe features.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! The `cursor_from_ptr` and `cursor_mut_from_ptr` allow you to create a
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//! cursor pointing to a specific element in the collection from a pointer to
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! that element. This is unsafe because it assumes that the objected pointed to
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//! is currently inserted in the collection.
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//!
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//! The `UnsafeRef` type acts like `Rc`, except without the reference count.
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//! Instead, you are responsible for keeping track of the number of active
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//! references to an object and for freeing it once the last reference is
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//! dropped. The advantage of `UnsafeRef` over `Rc` is that it reduces the size
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//! of the allocation by two `usize` and avoids the overhead of maintaining
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//! reference counts.
[270](https://docs.rs#270)
[271](https://docs.rs#271)#![warn(missing_docs)]
[272](https://docs.rs#272)#![warn(rust_2018_idioms)]
[273](https://docs.rs#273)#![no_std]
[274](https://docs.rs#274)#![cfg_attr(feature = "nightly", feature(const_fn_trait_bound))]

# AtomicLink in intrusive_collections::linked_list - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/intrusive-collections/latest/target-redirect/intrusive_collections/linked_list/struct.AtomicLink.html

`pub struct AtomicLink { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Intrusive atomic link that allows an object to be inserted into a
`LinkedList`. This link allows the structure to be shared between threads.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/intrusive_collections/linked_list.rs.html#289-331)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-AtomicLink)### impl [AtomicLink](https://docs.rs/struct.AtomicLink.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/intrusive_collections/linked_list.rs.html#289-331)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-AtomicLink)

### impl [AtomicLink](https://docs.rs/struct.AtomicLink.html)

Checks whether the `AtomicLink` is linked into a `LinkedList`.

Forcibly unlinks an object from a `LinkedList`.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

It is undefined behavior to call this function while still linked into a
`LinkedList`. The only situation where this function is useful is
after calling `fast_clear` on a `LinkedList`, since this clears
the collection without marking the nodes as unlinked.

Removes all elements from the `LinkedList`.

This will unlink all object currently in the list, which requires
iterating through all elements in the `LinkedList`. Each element is
converted back to an owned pointer and then dropped.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/intrusive_collections/linked_list.rs.html#1387-1390)#### pub fn [fast_clear](https://docs.rs#method.fast_clear)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/intrusive_collections/linked_list.rs.html#1387-1390)

#### pub fn [fast_clear](https://docs.rs#method.fast_clear)(&mut self)

Empties the `LinkedList` without unlinking or freeing objects in it.

Since this does not unlink any objects, any attempts to link these
objects into another `LinkedList` will fail but will not cause any
memory unsafety. To unlink those objects manually, you must call the
`force_unlink` function on them.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/intrusive_collections/linked_list.rs.html#1395-1407)#### pub fn [take](https://docs.rs#method.take)(&mut self) -> [LinkedList](https://docs.rs/struct.LinkedList.html)<A>

Takes all the elements out of the `LinkedList`, leaving it empty.
The taken elements are returned as a new `LinkedList`.

# RBTree in intrusive_collections::rbtree - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/intrusive-collections/latest/target-redirect/intrusive_collections/rbtree/struct.RBTree.html

`pub struct RBTree<A: `[Adapter](https://docs.rs/trait.Adapter.html)>{ /* private fields */ }## Expand description

An intrusive red-black tree.

When this collection is dropped, all elements linked into it will be converted back to owned pointers and dropped.

Note that you are responsible for ensuring that the elements in a `RBTree`
remain in ascending key order. This property can be violated, either because
the key of an element was modified, or because the
`insert_before`/`insert_after` methods of `CursorMut` were incorrectly used.
If this situation occurs, memory safety will not be violated but the `find`,
`upper_bound`, `lower_bound` and `range` may return incorrect results.

Removes all elements from the `RBTree`.

iterating through all elements in the `RBTree`. Each element is
converted back to an owned pointer and then dropped.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/intrusive_collections/rbtree.rs.html#1801-1803)#### pub fn [fast_clear](https://docs.rs#method.fast_clear)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/intrusive_collections/rbtree.rs.html#1801-1803)

#### pub fn [fast_clear](https://docs.rs#method.fast_clear)(&mut self)

Empties the `RBTree` without unlinking or freeing objects in it.

Since this does not unlink any objects, any attempts to link these
objects into another `RBTree` will fail but will not cause any
memory unsafety. To unlink those objects manually, you must call the
`force_unlink` function on them.

    &'a mut self,
    val: <A::[PointerOps](https://docs.rs/trait.Adapter.html#associatedtype.PointerOps) as [PointerOps](https://docs.rs/trait.PointerOps.html)>::[Pointer](https://docs.rs/trait.PointerOps.html#associatedtype.Pointer),
